verdict: Nvidia's founder quits; spies hand an AI agent the keys. A thin day for AI research.

posters.headline: Nvidia's founder quits as boss
posters.summary: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive officer (CEO) after weeks of reports about his private life and links to chip sales to China.
posters.soWhat: Work: key-person risk just hit the main supplier of AI chips.

photo.alt: Nvidia's headquarters building in Santa Clara, California.

posters.drawing: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 130" font-family="Arial,sans-serif"><line x1="20" y1="60" x2="320" y2="60" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="30" cy="60" r="6" fill="#333"/><text x="30" y="40" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">29 Oct</text><text x="30" y="88" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333" font-weight="normal">NYT report</text><circle cx="120" cy="60" r="6" fill="#333"/><text x="120" y="40" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">8 Nov</text><text x="120" y="88" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333" font-weight="normal">Apology</text><circle cx="210" cy="60" r="9" fill="#c2185b"/><text x="210" y="40" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">11 Nov</text><text x="210" y="88" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333" font-weight="bold">Resigns</text><circle cx="305" cy="60" r="6" fill="#333"/><text x="305" y="40" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333">17 Nov</text><text x="305" y="88" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#333" font-weight="normal">Results</text><text x="170" y="118" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#666">Shares down 11% over five days</text></svg>
posters.drawingAlt: Timeline: press report 29 October, staff apology 8 November, resignation 11 November, results due 17 November. Shares down 11% over five days.

read.what: Nvidia said on 12 November that Jensen Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. A filing showed the board accepted it on 11 November. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim CEO and keeps her finance role. Harvey C. Jones becomes the company's first chair of the board. TechCrunch reported shares fell about 8% after hours on 11 November and were down 11% over five days. Nvidia reports results on 17 November.
read.how: It followed two weeks of press reports. On 29 October The New York Times reported a close relationship between Mr Huang and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore firm investigated over suspected diversion of Nvidia chips to China. On 8 November he apologised to staff in a letter and the board began an independent investigation. On 11 November The Wall Street Journal reported the board was preparing to remove him. Nvidia's own release gives no reason.
read.why: Nvidia makes most of the chips that train and run today's AI systems, and Mr Huang led it for 33 years. A sudden change at the top, plus US congressional questions about chips reaching China, adds uncertainty for every AI programme that depends on its supply and roadmap. It also puts export-control compliance in the chip supply chain under a brighter light.
read.take: Opinion: products and contracts do not change overnight, so the near-term risk is slower decisions and closer scrutiny of China sales, not a supply shock. The claims about chip diversion are press reports, not findings, and Nvidia has said it had no reason to believe products were diverted. Watch the 17 November results call and who the board chooses.

posters.headline: Spies let an AI agent run the hack
posters.summary: A spy group linked to Kazakhstan used a self-hosted AI agent to search, steal and clean up inside Tajik government systems, an exposed server shows.
posters.soWhat: Work: attackers now give agents the keys. Add that to your threat model.

photo.alt: Dushanbe railway station in Tajikistan. Hackers had access to the national railway network for weeks.

read.what: Security firm CloudSEK found an exposed server used by a group it calls Silent Lynx and published its report on 11 November. The server held more than a dozen gigabytes across hundreds of thousands of files, including more than 2,000 unique stolen documents, mostly correspondence to or through Tajikistan's Ministry of Defence. The hackers had access to the national railway network from at least mid-August to early October, and used one employee's login to reach a national document system.
read.how: The operator ran a self-hosted AI agent called Hermes (an AI that runs tools on its own), mainly on a DeepSeek model reached through OpenRouter, a model marketplace. It did reconnaissance, gathered data and wiped logs. Its allowed-commands list let destructive commands run without a human approving them, and its stop-after-repeated-failures limit was switched off. Orders went in Russian through a Telegram bot, so it could be run from a phone. The clean-up missed the exposed folder.
read.why: It is a rare look at a real spy operation handing routine hacking work to an AI agent. The agent sped up the dull parts rather than inventing new attacks. It also shows the same safety settings defenders debate, approval steps and stop limits, being switched off by attackers. For any large organisation, it is a reminder that one stolen login can open a national system.
read.take: Opinion: the evidence is strong because it comes from the attacker's own logs, but it is one firm's report. CloudSEK rates the Kazakhstan link only medium confidence, and The Record notes the research shows no link to the Kazakh government. The root causes are old ones: stolen logins and weak monitoring. Watch for other security firms reporting agents in state hacking.

posters.headline: United bars AI agents from booking
posters.summary: United Airlines will block unauthorised personal AI assistants from booking flights or managing trips, warning that sharing logins with them exposes data.
posters.soWhat: Build: agents that log in as the user will meet more locked doors.

read.what: TechCrunch reported on 12 November that United will restrict AI agents that book flights and manage reservations for users. The block covers its own website and app, and travel agencies and aggregators. United said the aim is to 'prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants'. It is updating its booking, ticketing and distribution policies.
read.how: Many personal AI agents work by taking the user's password and acting inside their account (credential sharing). United gave no technical detail on how it will spot them; the stated tool is a policy change. It named three risks: exposed account details, accidental purchases or spent MileagePlus miles, and federal aviation rules, such as a passenger personally confirming at check-in that bags hold no banned items.
read.why: Booking travel is one of the flagship jobs AI agents are sold for. If big firms block agents that act on a user's login, agent makers will need approved routes, such as official partner connections (application programming interfaces, APIs). TechCrunch notes Bank of America recently urged customers not to share banking passwords with AI assistants.
read.take: Opinion: this is sound security, not hostility to AI. Giving an agent your password gives it every power you have, with no record of who did what. Expect more firms to split agents into approved ones, connected officially with limits, and the rest. Unknown: how United will tell an agent from a person. Watch whether other airlines follow.

stories.headline: Fireworks AI breach exposed Notion AI chat transcripts
stories.summary: Hackers who got into AI model host Fireworks through its cloud provider took chat transcripts from about 1% of Notion's customers who used one AI feature.
stories.soWhat: Work: your AI supplier's suppliers now sit in your data's path.

read.what: TechCrunch reported on 12 November that Notion confirmed hackers took chat transcripts from Notion AI customers who used its 'Insights' feature, about 1% of its customers. Fireworks AI, which runs AI models for other companies, said attackers took billing information and some datasets. It is Fireworks' second breach in about two months. Notion cut all connections to Fireworks on 3 November and deleted data stored there.
read.how: An attacker breached Fireworks' cloud provider and used that access to reach a Fireworks development system holding customer data. Notion sent some AI requests through Fireworks (a model hosting provider), so the transcripts, which include anything typed into or produced by the chat, sat in that chain. Fireworks believes the attackers want to sell stolen access to AI models (tokens) to people who will not pay for their own.
read.why: When you buy an AI feature, your words may pass through the vendor's model host and that host's cloud. Each link is a further supplier you never signed with. Notion says much of the data cannot be tied to particular customers, but chat transcripts often hold sensitive work content.
read.take: Opinion: this is AI supply chain risk in plain sight. Ask suppliers which model hosts see your prompts, how long they keep them and how fast you will be told of a breach. Fireworks, which says it has tens of thousands of customers, has not said how many were affected. Watch for that number.

stories.headline: Unpatched Windows flaw published with working attack code
stories.summary: A researcher released code that turns a 2025 Windows log-protection feature into a route to full SYSTEM control. Microsoft has issued no fix yet.
stories.soWhat: Work: ask IT how they will watch for this until Microsoft patches it.

read.what: On 10 November, the day of Microsoft's monthly updates, a researcher calling themselves MSNightmare posted proof-of-concept code and a write-up called SignDrop. The Hacker News reported on 12 November that it has no tracking number (CVE), advisory or patch. There are no reported attacks, and it is not on the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) list of exploited flaws.
read.how: In October 2025 Microsoft added a signing check to its Common Log File System driver (CLFS) to stop log tampering. SignDrop abuses it: when a privileged program opens a log the attacker prepared, Windows writes a side file with top-level (SYSTEM) rights, and a redirect (symbolic link) sends it where the attacker chooses. The ordinary user can still write to that file, which can be chained into full control (privilege escalation). The demo uses Microsoft Defender as the privileged program.
read.why: It needs an attacker already on the machine as a normal user, so it is a second-stage tool, the kind used after a phishing click. It was tested on Windows 11 26H2 and Windows Server 2025 test builds. The researcher says systems with the CLFS check switched off fall outside it.
read.take: Opinion: serious but not a panic. An independent tester found it works but not reliably, needs Defender running and changes every User Account Control (UAC) prompt, so it is noisy. Do not switch off the protection on your own. Watch for a Microsoft advisory and an out-of-cycle fix.

lessons.title: AlphaGo and learning by self-play
lessons.idea: AlphaGo learned Go by reinforcement learning: it played itself, scored each game as a win or loss, and shifted towards moves that won.
steps: First it copied moves from expert human games (supervised learning).
Then it played different versions of itself thousands of times (self-play).
Each game ends in a win or a loss: the only score it gets (the reward).
It nudges its move-picker (policy network) towards moves that led to wins.
A second network (value network) learns to guess who is winning from a position.
In a match, a look-ahead search (Monte Carlo tree search) uses both networks.
lessons.analogy: Picture a tennis player with no coach who plays thousands of practice sets against a copy of themselves. Nobody tells them which shot was good. They only see who won each set, and slowly they play more of the shots that turned up in winning sets. Some of those shots look odd to watching experts, because the player was never taught what 'normal' looks like.
lessons.breaks: A person learns from a handful of games and from explanations. AlphaGo needed huge numbers of games, a perfectly clear score and a world with fixed rules. Real work rarely gives a clean win or loss at the end, and you cannot replay a client meeting thousands of times. That is why self-play shines in games and code, where results are easy to check.
lessons.why: In March 2016 AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4-1 in Seoul, a match DeepMind says over 200 million people watched. In game two, move 37 had, by DeepMind's account, a 1 in 10,000 chance of being played, and it helped win the game. It showed that learning from outcomes can find ideas outside human data. The same idea, rewarding results, helps explain why coding agents improve fast: tests give a clear pass or fail.

lessons.title: Risk as likelihood times impact
lessons.idea: Score a risk as likelihood (1 to 5) times impact (1 to 5) on a 5 by 5 grid, but know that equal scores can hide very different risks.
steps: Rate how likely the event is, from 1 (rare) to 5 (almost certain).
Rate how bad it would be, from 1 (minor) to 5 (severe).
Multiply: likelihood 4 x impact 2 = 8; likelihood 1 x impact 5 = 5.
Plot each risk on the 5 by 5 grid; darker squares get attention first.
Then ask what the score hides: a rare disaster can score below a common nuisance.
lessons.analogy: It is like a weather forecast that multiplies the chance of rain by how wet you would get. Light drizzle that is very likely and a rare cloudburst can come out with similar numbers, yet you would pack very differently for each.
lessons.breaks: Weather has decades of data behind each number. Cyber risk scores are usually expert guesses on a short scale. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) guide SP 800-30 Revision 1 (September 2012) warns that such scales have a small range, which makes ranking risks hard, and that different experts may reach very different results unless each level is clearly defined.
lessons.why: Almost every risk register you will meet uses this grid, and NIST describes risk as typically a function of impact and likelihood. Use it to start a conversation, not to end one. When two risks score 8, ask which one could end the business. Rare, severe risks (likelihood 1, impact 5) often deserve more than their score of 5 suggests, such as a tested recovery plan.

diagram.alt: A 5 by 5 grid, likelihood across and impact up, shading darker towards the top right. Risk A sits at 4 by 2 = 8, risk C at 2 by 4 = 8, and risk B at 1 by 5 = 5, showing equal scores can be different risks.

lessons.title: Bytes, hexadecimal and sizes
lessons.idea: A byte is 8 bits. Split it into two 4-bit halves and each half is one hex digit, so 11111111 = FF = 255, and #FF0000 is pure red.
steps: A byte is 8 bits, so it can hold 256 values: 0 to 255.
Split the byte into two 4-bit halves (nibbles); each half holds 0 to 15.
Hexadecimal (base 16) counts 0 to 9, then A to F, so one digit covers one nibble: 1111 = F.
So 11111111 = FF = 15 x 16 + 15 = 255. The 0x prefix marks hex, as in 0xFF.
A web colour #RRGGBB is three bytes: #FF0000 is red full on, green and blue off.
Sizes: a megabyte (MB) is 1,000,000 bytes; a mebibyte (MiB) is 1,048,576.
lessons.analogy: Think of a byte as an eight-digit combination lock where each wheel shows only 0 or 1. Hex is shorthand that reads the lock in two halves, giving each half a single symbol from 0 to F, so eight wheels become two characters.
lessons.breaks: A lock combination means nothing by itself, while a byte's meaning depends on how a program reads it: the same FF could be the number 255, part of a colour or part of a letter. Hex is only a way of writing bits for humans; the computer still stores 1s and 0s.
lessons.why: Hex turns up in colour codes, memory addresses, security hashes and error codes. Harvard's CS50 notes that hex is used because it shows information more compactly. File sizes matter when you set upload limits or budget cloud storage: the International Electrotechnical Commission set binary prefixes such as mebi in 1998 because 'megabyte' was being used for both 1,000,000 and 1,048,576 bytes.

lessons.title: A model is a function with dials
lessons.idea: A model is a function, such as price = w x size + b, whose adjustable numbers (parameters) are turned until its output fits real examples.
steps: Choose the rule's shape: y = w x + b, a straight line.
x is the input (house size) and y is the output (predicted price).
w (a weight) sets the slope; b (a bias) sets where the line starts.
With toy dials w = 2 and b = 1, a size of 3 gives 2 x 3 + 1 = 7.
Measure the error against real examples (a cost function, such as least squares).
Turn the dials a little to shrink the error, and repeat (gradient descent).
lessons.analogy: It is like tuning an old radio with two knobs. One knob moves the needle quickly, the other shifts the starting point. You listen, turn a little, listen again, until the station is clear. The station is the pattern in the data.
lessons.breaks: A radio has one right station and you can hear when you have found it. A model only ever gets close on the examples it saw, and it can fit them well yet still be wrong on new cases. Large models also have vastly more dials than two, and nobody turns them by hand.
lessons.why: Stanford's CS229 notes start with exactly this: 47 houses in Portland, Oregon, price predicted from living area. Gradient descent tuned the two parameters to 71.27 and 0.1345 (price in $1000s). The language models you use are the same idea at enormous scale: a fixed shape, and parameters tuned by data. When someone says a model 'learned', they mean its dials moved.

lessons.title: Quantitative risk: annualised loss expectancy
lessons.idea: Annualised loss expectancy (ALE) is the cost of one incident times how often it happens a year; compare it with what a control costs a year.
steps: Asset value (AV): what the thing at risk is worth.
Exposure factor (EF): the share of that value one incident destroys.
Single loss expectancy: SLE = AV x EF, the cost of one incident.
Annual rate of occurrence (ARO): incidents a year; once in five years = 0.2.
ALE = SLE x ARO: £400,000 x 0.2 = £80,000 a year.
Compare with the control: £50,000 a year is worth it if it removes enough loss.
lessons.analogy: It is like deciding whether to insure a phone. If a broken screen costs £200 and you break one about every two years, you expect to lose £100 a year. A cover costing £60 a year looks good; one costing £150 does not.
lessons.breaks: With phones you have years of your own history. With cyber events, the rate is often a guess and one bad year can be far worse than the average. ALE also treats a likely small loss and a rare huge loss the same if they multiply to the same number, which is the grid's blind spot again.
lessons.why: Boards and finance teams think in money, not colours. ALE lets you say 'this control costs £50,000 and should save about £80,000 a year'. Be honest: compare the control's cost with how much it reduces the ALE, not the whole ALE. A worked example from Destination Certification: a $2,000 camera system, 10% damage per voltage spike, 3 spikes a year, gives an ALE of $600.

diagram.alt: Two bars: a control costing £50,000 a year, and a longer bar for ALE of 0.2 x £400,000 = £80,000. If the control stops all of it, you are £30,000 ahead; if it stops half, £10,000 behind.

quiz.q: When AlphaGo played against itself, what feedback did it get?
options: A human coach marking each move
Only whether each game ended in a win or a loss
A list of the strongest opening moves from Go books
The number of stones captured on every turn
quiz.why: Self-play gives one clear signal at the end: win or lose. Reinforcement learning shifts the networks towards moves that led to wins, which is how odd but strong moves like 37 appear.

quiz.q: Risk A is likelihood 4, impact 2. Risk C is likelihood 2, impact 4. What does the 5 by 5 grid hide?
options: C scores 16 because impact counts double on the grid
Both score 8, but one is frequent and minor, one rarer and worse
Likelihood always matters more than impact, so A wins
Equal scores mean the two risks need exactly the same response plan
quiz.why: 4 x 2 and 2 x 4 both make 8, so the grid ranks them equally. But a frequent nuisance and a rarer, more damaging event usually need different responses.

quiz.q: In the web colour code #00FF00, what does the FF tell the screen?
options: Turn red fully on and leave the others off
Turn blue to half strength
Turn green fully on, 255 out of 255
Make the colour 255% brighter
quiz.why: #RRGGBB is three bytes. The middle pair is green, and FF is 15 x 16 + 15 = 255, the most one byte holds. So #00FF00 is pure green.

quiz.q: In y = w x + b, starting from w = 2 and b = 1, what does training change?
options: The input x, until it matches the price
The formula's shape, from a line to a curve
Nothing at all, because a programmer sets the dials by hand
The dials w and b, until the line fits the examples
quiz.why: x is the data you feed in. Training keeps the shape and turns the parameters w and b to shrink the error, for example by gradient descent.

quiz.q: One breach would cost £400,000 and is expected once every five years. What is the annualised loss expectancy?
options: £80,000 a year
£50,000 a year
quiz.why: Once in five years is a yearly rate of 0.2. ALE = £400,000 x 0.2 = £80,000 a year, which you then compare with what a control costs and saves.

quiz.title: Counting in binary
quiz.q: What is the binary number 1011 in decimal?
quiz.why: Read the columns from the right as 1, 2, 4 and 8. 1011 has an 8, no 4, a 2 and a 1: 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.

quiz.title: The CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity, availability
quiz.q: Ransomware locks a hospital's records so staff cannot open them. Which property broke first?
options: Confidentiality
Integrity
Authenticity
Availability
quiz.why: Staff cannot reach what they need, so availability broke. Gangs that also steal files hit confidentiality too, but locking people out is an attack on availability.

terms.plain: Learning by trying things and being rewarded for good outcomes, such as winning a game.
A program improving by playing against copies of itself.
A 5 by 5 grid that scores a risk as likelihood times impact.
Base 16 counting with 0 to 9 and A to F. Two hex digits describe one byte.
An adjustable number inside a model, tuned by data. Also called a weight.
Expected yearly cost of a risk: the cost of one incident times how often it happens a year.
An AI system that runs tools and takes steps on its own towards a goal.
Turning limited access on a computer into higher, often full, control.

build.title: A risk scorer that shows its blind spots
build.idea: A one-page web tool where you enter a risk's likelihood, impact, single loss and yearly rate. It shows the 5 by 5 grid score and the yearly money loss side by side, and flags rare, severe risks the grid underrates.
build.first: Ask Claude to build one HTML page with four number boxes that calculates likelihood times impact and single loss times yearly rate, then test it with the 4 x 2 and 1 x 5 examples.

chatter.headline: Nvidia's open car AI decides in under 0.2 seconds, it says
chatter.summary: Nvidia released Alpamayo 2 Edge, an open model that plans a car's path on board and can explain its choices. People are weighing whether a small model can be safe enough.
chatter.insight: Nvidia says the 2 billion parameter model goes from camera pixels to a planned path in 160 to 190 milliseconds on its DRIVE AGX Thor computer, small enough to run inside the car.
chatter.dissent: All results come from Nvidia's own simulator, and one write-up quoted 40 times fewer errors where Nvidia's blog says about 60 times. Real-road safety is unproven.
chatter.trustNote: Opened Nvidia's developer blog (10 Nov): 2B parameters, 160 to 190 ms, about 60 times the distance between at-fault incidents in its own simulator. No independent test found.

chatter.headline: Coding is changing faster than any profession before it
chatter.summary: A business school professor argues coding is the exception to slow AI adoption: the profession is being transformed less than a year after working coding agents arrived.
chatter.insight: Coding has clear checks, such as tests that pass or fail, which makes agents easier to trust and adopt than in fields where good work is harder to judge.
chatter.dissent: It is an opinion with no data in the post. Fast tool adoption is not the same as a transformed profession, and other fields may simply lack measurable checks.
chatter.trustNote: A single opinion post with no source to open. Read it as one informed view, not a finding.

builds.what: A bridge that lets Claude Code ask Antigravity agents for reviews
builds.label: CODE REVIEW
steps: You ask Claude Code for a review; it writes the code and runs the tests first.
It starts a reviewer agent in Google Antigravity through a small server (an MCP server).
The reviewer reads the project, runs tests and returns a structured list of findings.
Claude fixes what it agrees with, disputes the rest, and they repeat until they agree.
builds.proof_note: Opened the public GitHub repository: MIT licence, 11 commits, and a note that it is not affiliated with Google or Anthropic.
builds.level_note: Free code, but you need Claude Code and Antigravity set up and some comfort typing terminal commands.
builds.first_step: Read the four setup commands in the README, then try one review on a small practice project, not on real work.
